newsitem.title: UK: Patten not to run for UK Conservative leader - Sky TV.
newsitem.headline: Patten not to run for UK Conservative leader - Sky TV.

text.p: Hong Kong governor Chris Patten has ruled himself out of the race to be the next leader of Britain's Conservative Party, Sky television news reported on Saturday.

Sky said Patten had told them he was "flattered" by suggestions he could take over from John Major, defeated in Thursday's election, but would take time off after his job as governor ends on June 30 to write a book.
"The only plans I have at present are to take six or seven months off after the handover of Hong Kong to write a book about Asia and Europe," Sky quoted Patten as saying.

Major said on Friday he would resign the party leadership after his party was routed by Labour in the polls but so far, only former finance minister Kenneth Clarke has entered what promises to be a closely fought race.
Others are believed to be mulling their chances.
Outgoing Welsh Secretary William Hague, 36, and Major's former deputy Michael Heseltine, 64, are possible contenders.
Former health secretary Stephen Dorrell has said he will discuss the matter with colleagues and outgoing interior minister Michael Howard might also throw in his cap.
John Redwood, the 45-year-old former cabinet minister who challenged Major for the leadership two years ago, is considered the front-runner on the Euro-sceptic right of the party.
But with Patten out of the fray, the list of high-profile moderates has shrunk measurably.
The mastermind of Major's election victory in 1992 -- when he lost his own west of England seat in Bath -- Patten remains a close friend to Major, who gave him the Hong Kong job.

He was tipped as a potential successor for his moderate politics and ability to return to politics unsullied by the infighting that has split the Conservatives in their disastrous election campaign. A staunch Catholic, he was seen as a man who could re-group the party in its new-found state of opposition.

Conservative MP Michael Colvin said earlier on Saturday that a member of parliament with a safe seat should stand aside for the former party chairman to take up on his return from Hong Kong after Britain returns power to China this summer.
Sky said Patten appreciated Colvin's "kind" suggestion but would not be taking up the offer.
Patten also won the endorsement on Saturday of Britain's new Labour foreign minister, appointed to the job on Friday.

"Foreign Secretary Robin Cook confirmed today that Chris Patten would remain governor of Hong Kong until the handover on June 30. He had complete confidence in Mr Patten and looked forward to working with him in the interests of the people of Hong Kong," said a Foreign Office spokesman.
